procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court dated 21.09.2023
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court heard a petition under Section 482 CrPC.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remanded the matter back to the High Court, directing it to convert the petition under Section 482 CrPC into a criminal revision under Section 397 CrPC and decide it in accordance with law after affording opportunity of hearing to the parties.

directions: The impugned order of the High Court dated 21.09.2023 is set aside.
The matter is remanded to the High Court.
The High Court is directed to convert the petition under Section 482 CrPC as a criminal revision under Section 397 CrPC.
The High Court is directed to decide the matter in accordance with law after affording opportunity of hearing to the parties.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court can convert the petition u/s.482 CrPC into a revision u/s.397 CrPC and decide it as per law;

facts: An appellant-wife, dissatisfied with the amount of interim maintenance she was awarded, filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) seeking an enhancement.

The High Court dismissed her petition, not on its merits, but on the grounds that it was not maintainable because she had an alternative remedy available: filing a revision petition under Section 397 CrPC.
law: The Supreme Court cited a 'catena of decisions' (a series of previous rulings) establishing that the nomenclature (or title) of a petition is immaterial.
To ensure substantive justice is done, a High Court has the power to convert a petition filed under Section 482 CrPC into a revision under Section 397 CrPC, and vice versa.

The availability of an alternative remedy, such as a revision under Section 397, is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to dismiss a petition filed under the High Court's inherent powers in Section 482.

The Court referenced its ruling in *Prabhu Chawla v. State of Rajasthan*, which held that nothing in the CrPC, including Section 397, can limit the broad amplitude of the inherent powers granted to the High Court under Section 482.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's dismissal of the petition was based on a 'hyper technical ground' and was not a 'judicious approach'.
It reasoned that even if the High Court believed a revision under Section 397 was the more appropriate procedure, it should not have simply dismissed the case ('non-suited the appellant').
The correct course of action would have been for the High Court to exercise its power to convert the Section 482 petition into a Section 397 revision and then decide the case on its merits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court can and should convert a petition under Section 482 CrPC into a revision under Section 397 CrPC to serve the ends of justice. It set aside the High Court's order and remanded the matter with a specific direction to convert the petition into a criminal revision and decide it in accordance with the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether s.397 CrPC can affect the amplitude of the inherent powers of the High Court u/s. 482 CrPC.

facts: A wife filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) in the High Court, seeking to enhance her interim maintenance.
The High Court dismissed this petition, reasoning that it was not maintainable because the wife had an alternative remedy available: filing a revision petition under Section 397 CrPC.
law: The Supreme Court cited its previous ruling in *Prabhu Chawla v. State of Rajasthan*, which held that nothing in the CrPC, including Section 397, can affect or limit the broad scope (amplitude) of the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482.
The Court also noted that the availability of an alternative remedy, such as a revision under Section 397, is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to dismiss an application under Section 482.

The Court reiterated the principle from a series of decisions that the nomenclature or label of a petition is immaterial, and the High Court can convert a petition from one section to another (e.g., from s.482 to s.397) to ensure substantive justice is done.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's dismissal of the petition was based on a "hyper technical ground" and was not a judicious approach.
It applied the principle from *Prabhu Chawla*, stating that the existence of the revisional power under Section 397 does not act as a bar on the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482.

The Court reasoned that instead of dismissing the petition, the High Court should have focused on substantive justice. The proper course of action would have been to convert the wife's Section 482 petition into a Section 397 revision petition and then decide the case on its merits.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that Section 397 CrPC can affect the amplitude of the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC. It held that the availability of a revisional remedy under Section 397 is not a valid reason to dismiss a petition under Section 482, as the inherent powers of the High Court remain unaffected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court can convert the petition u/s.482 CrPC into a revision u/s.397 CrPC and decide it as per law;
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court should not have dismissed their petition under Section 482 CrPC on the ground of an alternative remedy being available.
The appellant contended that the judicious approach would have been for the High Court to convert the petition into a revision under Section 397 CrPC and decide it on its merits.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not appear before the court and therefore made no arguments.

appellant_arguments: The appellant's position, by filing under Section 482 and appealing the dismissal, was that the availability of a remedy under Section 397 CrPC does not bar or diminish the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not appear before the court and therefore made no arguments.

cases.case_name: Madhu Limaye v. The State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: As part of a 'catena of decisions' establishing that the nomenclature of a petition is immaterial and for doing substantive justice, the High Court can convert a petition under Section 482 CrPC to a revision under Section 397 CrPC and vice versa.

cases.case_name: Prabhu Chawla v. State of Rajasthan and Another
cases.principle: As part of a 'catena of decisions' establishing that the nomenclature of a petition is immaterial and for doing substantive justice, the High Court can convert a petition under Section 482 CrPC to a revision under Section 397 CrPC and vice versa.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court should not dismiss a petition filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) solely on the ground that an alternative remedy under Section 397 CrPC is available; the judicious approach is to convert the petition to the appropriate provision and decide it in accordance with the law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that even if the High Court believed a petition should have been filed under its revisional jurisdiction (Section 397 CrPC) instead of its inherent jurisdiction (Section 482 CrPC), it should not have dismissed the petition solely on the ground that an alternative remedy was available. The proper and judicious course of action would have been for the High Court to convert the petition from one under Section 482 CrPC into a revision under Section 397 CrPC and then decide the matter on its merits.
legal_tests_applied: The court's reasoning was guided by precedents establishing the relationship between the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC and its revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 CrPC, specifically citing Madhu Limaye v. The State of Maharashtra and Prabhu Chawla v. State of Rajasthan and Another.
policy_considerations: The court emphasized that a 'judicious approach' requires preventing a party from being 'non-suited' (denied a hearing on the merits) merely for choosing the incorrect procedural remedy when a simple conversion to the correct one is possible. This promotes substantive justice over procedural technicalities.
